text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Imagine a woman in Nairobi who runs a small market stall selling fabric. She's been in business for six years. She pays her suppliers on time, she pays her phone bill every month, and she moves money through mobile payments every day. She wants a loan to buy more stock before the holiday season.

speaker: JAMES
text: And the lender's first question is simple. Can we trust her to pay it back? In a country like Britain or the United States, the lender would look her up in a credit bureau and see a long history of loans and repayments. But she's never had a bank loan. On paper, she barely exists.

speaker: NORA
text: So the lender either says no, or charges her a very high rate to cover the risk, or finds some other way to see what she's really like as a borrower.

speaker: JAMES
text: That "other way" is what today's company is built around. Making it possible for lenders, in markets where credit information is thin, to make better decisions about who to trust.

speaker: NORA
text: Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. We've spent the last few episodes in the world of law and disputes. Today we change gear completely, with Creditinfo, a credit bureau and credit decisioning group with roots in Iceland and operations across Africa, the Caribbean, the Baltics and beyond.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: company pages, press releases, trade press and the private equity firm's own announcements. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a number comes from the company, we'll flag it. And nothing here is financial, legal or investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And since we'll be talking about credit scoring, I'd add that nothing we say is advice on how to improve your own credit. We're talking about the business, not your loan application.

speaker: NORA
text: Good. So, James. Creditinfo in one sentence.

speaker: JAMES
text: Creditinfo runs credit bureaus and sells credit data, fraud and identity checks, and lending decision software to banks, lenders and governments, mainly in emerging and frontier markets, and it has been majority owned by Levine Leichtman since March 2021.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three reasons. It has been buying fast, including a Caribbean bureau group in August 2026. It's sitting on exactly the kind of data that AI in lending and compliance runs on. And yet, from the outside, it doesn't have a named AI product. So it's a company with a very valuable data asset, and an open question about how it turns that into AI-era products.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. Where and when was it founded?

speaker: JAMES
text: It was founded in 1997, according to both the company and the private equity firm. The founder is Reynir Grétarsson, an Icelander, who was the majority shareholder until 2021. And here's an unusual wrinkle. We're not quite sure where it's headquartered today.

speaker: NORA
text: How can you not know where a company is headquartered?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because the sources disagree. The private equity firm's portfolio page and the 2021 deal pages say Reykjavik, Iceland. The company's own website and its 2026 press releases say London. Our guess is that the group has moved its main base to London, or that it describes itself differently in different places. But we can't confirm which, so I'll say roots in Reykjavik, and a strong London presence today.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is it?

speaker: JAMES
text: The company's website says about four hundred and eighty employees, though the page isn't dated. It says it serves more than forty countries, while the private equity firm's page says it has bureau operations in twenty-three countries. Those two can both be true: running a bureau in a country is different from selling services into it. The website also says it has reached more than a million clients, but the wording is unclear, so I wouldn't lean on that number. Revenue isn't public.

speaker: NORA
text: Who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: The global chief executive is Satrajit Saha, appointed at the end of November 2023. Before that he was chief executive of TransUnion Europe. TransUnion is one of the three big global credit bureaus, alongside Experian and Equifax. So he brings large-bureau experience to a company that often competes in markets the big bureaus have left. The founder, Reynir Grétarsson, kept a board seat and a significant minority stake after the 2021 deal. And Kristinn Agnarsson has been chief executive of EveryData, the Caribbean group it just bought, since 2020.

speaker: NORA
text: What about technology leadership? A chief technology officer, a head of AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find those names in public sources. That doesn't mean the roles don't exist, but it's one of the gaps in the picture.

speaker: NORA
text: Iceland is a small country. How does a credit bureau from Iceland end up in Uganda and the Caribbean?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a detailed company history, so this is partly our reading. But it's a pattern you see in some small-country companies. When your home market is tiny, you learn to build systems that are efficient and adaptable, and then you look abroad very early for growth. A company that knows how to run a full credit bureau for a small population has a product that suits other small and mid-sized markets well. The 2021 press coverage described the group as having around thirty locations, which tells you how international it already was by then.

speaker: NORA
text: So being small at home was almost an advantage.

speaker: JAMES
text: In a way. The big bureaus built their systems for huge markets like the United States and Britain. A bureau designed for a country of a few hundred thousand people may be a better fit for, say, Namibia or a Caribbean island than a giant's platform. That's our inference, but it would help explain why Creditinfo has been the natural buyer when Experian has sold smaller operations.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the ownership history.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's short. Founder-owned from 1997 until March 2021, when Levine Leichtman bought a majority stake, with the founder and management partnering on the deal. The deal was announced and closed on the ninth of March 2021. The value wasn't disclosed, and the investment bank Alantra advised on the sell side.

speaker: NORA
text: So about five years and eight months into the hold.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right, and that's significant. In private equity, five to six years is a mature hold. People start thinking about what the next owner will want to see. And, in my view, a buyer looking at a data business in 2027 or 2028 will ask a very pointed question: what's your AI story?

speaker: NORA
text: What has it bought under the current owner?

speaker: JAMES
text: Quite a lot, and the pattern is interesting. In May 2023 it bought the credit bureaus in Uganda and Namibia from Experian. It also bought an Estonian credit bureau from Experian, though we couldn't find the date. In April 2026 it took its stake in KIB Latvia, a Latvian credit bureau, from fifty-one percent to full ownership. And in August 2026 it completed the acquisition of EveryData Group, which runs credit bureaus in eleven Caribbean countries and offers advisory services.

speaker: NORA
text: Three of those came from Experian.

speaker: JAMES
text: Which tells you something. One of the biggest bureaus in the world chose to sell operations in some smaller markets, and Creditinfo was the buyer. Our reading is that the global players are concentrating on their largest markets, and that creates an opening for a specialist that wants to be excellent in smaller ones.

speaker: NORA
text: And there's more than acquisitions. You mentioned governments.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. In February 2026 Creditinfo Central Africa began operating the regional credit information bureau for CEMAC, the economic and monetary community of six Central African countries. The company has also been associated with the BIC-UEMOA regional bureau in West Africa, according to its news pages. These are big, government-backed contracts to run national or regional credit infrastructure.

speaker: NORA
text: So sometimes the customer isn't a bank at all, it's a central bank or a regional authority.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. In many emerging markets, setting up a credit bureau is a policy decision, made to widen access to credit. Regulators or regional bodies choose a technology and operating partner, often through a tender. Being that partner gives you a licence, a long-term position and a very strong data asset.

speaker: NORA
text: What does running a regional bureau actually involve?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, quite a lot. You build or adapt the technology that collects data from every participating lender, often banks and microfinance institutions in several countries. You set data standards so that a loan in one country is recorded the same way as a loan in another. You check data quality, because lenders submit errors. You handle disputes when a borrower says their file is wrong. And you produce reports and scores that lenders trust. In a region like CEMAC, you do that across several countries with shared regulation, which adds complexity.

speaker: NORA
text: And then the data has to be protected.

speaker: JAMES
text: Absolutely. A regional bureau holds sensitive financial information on a lot of people. Security, access control and compliance with each country's rules are part of the job from the first day. And because these contracts are often with public bodies, the bureau operator is under scrutiny from regulators and, sometimes, the press.

speaker: NORA
text: And EveryData. Tell me more about that one.

speaker: JAMES
text: EveryData Group runs credit bureaus in eleven Caribbean countries and also offers advisory services, according to the trade press coverage of the deal, which completed in August 2026. Its chief executive since 2020 is Kristinn Agnarsson. The Caribbean is a good example of the kind of market Creditinfo likes: many small, separate island economies, each with its own regulator and its own lenders, where a specialist that can run bureaus efficiently across all of them has an edge over a giant that would find each one too small to bother with.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back and explain what a credit bureau actually does, because I think most people only know them as the company that gives them a score.

speaker: JAMES
text: At its simplest, a credit bureau collects information about how people and businesses borrow and repay. Banks and other lenders share data about their customers' loans: how much, what type, whether payments are on time. The bureau combines that information from many lenders into one file per person or business. When a lender is deciding whether to lend, it asks the bureau for the applicant's report, and often for a score that summarises the risk.

speaker: NORA
text: Why would banks share their data with each other, effectively?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because everyone benefits. If you only know how a borrower has treated you, you might miss that they've just taken out five other loans elsewhere and are falling behind on all of them. Pooling information through a bureau reduces bad lending across the whole system. In many countries, sharing is required by regulation.

speaker: NORA
text: And then there's business information.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. Bureaus also hold data on companies: who owns them, who runs them, how they pay their suppliers, whether they've defaulted. That's useful for lending to small businesses, and also for checking who you're dealing with. And that leads to a third area, which is identity and compliance. Before a bank opens an account, it has to verify who the customer is, and check whether they're on sanctions lists or are a politically exposed person.

speaker: NORA
text: Explain politically exposed person.

speaker: JAMES
text: A politically exposed person, often shortened to PEP, is someone in a prominent public role, or close to someone who is, like a minister, a senior official or their family. Banks are required to apply extra scrutiny to them, because of the higher risk of corruption and money laundering. Checking customers against those lists is part of what's called know your customer, or KYC, and anti-money laundering, or AML.

speaker: NORA
text: So Creditinfo's product lines are...

speaker: JAMES
text: In its own words, consumer and business credit bureaus, KYC and PEP data and business information, fraud and identity, and decisioning software. That last one is important. It's not just selling the data, it's selling the software that lenders use to make the decision, applying their own rules and scores to the bureau data.

speaker: NORA
text: Why does decisioning software matter so much?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because it moves you from being a data supplier to being part of the lender's workflow. A data feed can be swapped for another one. Software that runs your entire loan approval process is much harder to replace. And it's the natural home for AI models in lending.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the markets. Why would a company focus on Uganda, Namibia, Latvia or the Caribbean rather than the big markets?

speaker: JAMES
text: A few reasons, in my view. First, the big markets are taken. In the United States and Britain, the three big bureaus are entrenched. Competing head on is very hard. Second, frontier markets are where credit is growing fastest. Digital lending through mobile phones has expanded access to credit in many African countries, and lenders need data to make those decisions safely.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, policy. Many governments and regional bodies want to widen access to credit, what's often called financial inclusion. Creditinfo's own mission is framed around that. When a country decides it needs a modern credit bureau, a specialist with experience setting them up in other countries has a real advantage.

speaker: NORA
text: And the licences are a moat.

speaker: JAMES
text: In our view, yes. Credit bureaus are licensed and regulated in each country. Getting a licence, building trust with the central bank and the lenders, and collecting years of repayment data takes a long time. That's very hard for a new entrant to replicate quickly.

speaker: NORA
text: But the data in those markets is thinner.

speaker: JAMES
text: Much thinner. That's the challenge and the opportunity. In a market where most adults have never had a formal loan, a traditional bureau file is empty for most people. That's why alternative data matters so much. Things like mobile money transactions, phone bill payments, and the records of fintech lenders. In June 2025 Creditinfo announced partnerships in Kenya with Kamoa and Little App, two local companies, around credit access and financial inclusion.

speaker: NORA
text: And that's the woman from the cold open.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's exactly her. If a bureau can include signals from the kinds of payments she makes every day, with her consent and within the rules, a lender can see her as a reliable person rather than a blank file.

speaker: NORA
text: Why is Kenya such a focus for this kind of thing?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, Kenya is widely known as one of the pioneers of mobile money, where people send, receive and store money through their phones, often without a bank account. That created a huge digital record of everyday financial behaviour, and a wave of digital lenders offering small loans through apps. It also created problems, like people taking several small loans from different apps at once. Good bureau data helps lenders see that, and helps responsible borrowers get better terms.

speaker: NORA
text: So the same technology that widens access can create new risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Which is why a strong, neutral credit information system matters more, not less, as digital lending grows.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make it concrete. Walk me through a loan decision. An invented example, not a real lender or person.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Let's call our stallholder Grace, and the lender a mid-sized digital lender in Kenya, call it Jua Credit. Grace downloads Jua's app on a Tuesday afternoon and applies for a loan of, say, a few hundred dollars' worth of Kenyan shillings, to be repaid over three months.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What happens first?
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Identity. The app asks for her national ID number and a selfie. In the background, Jua checks that the ID is real, that it matches the face, and that the phone number has been linked to her for a while, rather than being a new SIM card a fraudster just bought. Some of those checks might come from a bureau, some from a specialist identity provider.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Then credit.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Then Jua's decisioning system asks the bureau for Grace's report. Let's say it shows one small loan from a microfinance institution four years ago, repaid on time, and nothing else. Traditionally, that's a thin file. Jua's rules might say: not enough history, decline, or approve a tiny amount at a high rate.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: But if there's alternative data?
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Then the picture changes. Suppose, with Grace's consent, the bureau also has information from a fintech partner showing years of regular mobile payments and on-time bill payments. The score now reflects a reliable person with a stable small business. Jua's system approves a larger amount at a lower rate. All of this happens in a minute or two.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And then the loan is repaid, or not.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Right, and that's the important part. Jua reports Grace's repayments back to the bureau each month. If she repays on time, her file gets richer, and the next lender sees a stronger borrower. That's the virtuous circle a credit bureau creates. Over time, more people move from invisible to visible, and lending becomes safer and cheaper.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Where's the AI in that story?
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Potentially in several places. In the identity and fraud checks, spotting patterns that suggest a fake application. In the scoring itself, using machine learning to make better predictions from thin and alternative data. And in the decisioning software, helping the lender set its rules and monitor how its loans perform. Creditinfo has a foot in all of those. The question is how much of the AI it owns.
chapter: A loan decision, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: How big is this market?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a reliable figure. The only number we came across was a press release headline from a market research firm claiming a very large global figure, and frankly it wasn't credible enough to repeat. So I'll just say that credit information is a large global industry, dominated by a few giants, with many smaller national and regional players.

speaker: NORA
text: Who are the giants?

speaker: JAMES
text: Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, the three big global bureaus. Experian has sold several smaller operations to Creditinfo, as we discussed. TransUnion is where the chief executive used to work. And Equifax is now both a competitor and a partner.

speaker: NORA
text: A partner how?

speaker: JAMES
text: In July 2026 Creditinfo and Equifax announced a strategic partnership to give Creditinfo's customers access to Equifax's Kount 360 platform, for digital fraud detection. That's things like bots, credential stuffing, where attackers try stolen passwords at scale, and account takeover, across ten European countries. Interestingly, the announcement didn't use the words AI or machine learning at all. The company has also said it's exploring taking that partnership into Africa and the Middle East.

speaker: NORA
text: So in some places they compete and in others they cooperate.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's increasingly normal in data businesses. Creditinfo has the local presence and the bureau licences. Equifax has a global fraud platform. Together they offer customers something neither could alone in those markets. The risk, in my view, is that the partner captures a lot of the value.

speaker: NORA
text: Who else is in the picture?

speaker: JAMES
text: A newer group of AI-native companies. Lucinity, which is an AI-powered compliance platform for KYC and transaction monitoring. In May 2025 Creditinfo and Lucinity announced a partnership to feed Creditinfo's KYC and PEP data into Lucinity's AI compliance workflows. Facctum, which does AI-powered real-time watchlist screening and has partnered with Lucinity. And CredoLab, which does AI credit scoring using alternative data. We only saw those last two through headlines, so I'll keep it at that.

speaker: NORA
text: So Lucinity is a partner too.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's both a partner and, potentially, a channel competitor. Creditinfo supplies data. Lucinity runs the AI workflow that the bank's compliance team uses every day. If the bank's relationship is with Lucinity, Creditinfo risks becoming one of several data feeds plugged in behind it.

speaker: NORA
text: And then there's fraud more broadly.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. In November 2025 Creditinfo announced a partnership with NOTO for fraud and anti-money laundering controls. Put that together with Equifax Kount and Lucinity, and you can see a clear direction. Bureaus are moving beyond credit data into fraud, identity and compliance. That's where a lot of the demand is, as digital lending and digital banking grow.

speaker: NORA
text: Why is fraud growing so fast?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, because more of finance is digital. When you open an account on your phone without visiting a branch, the bank has to be sure you're who you say you are. Fraudsters use stolen identities, synthetic identities made by combining real and fake details, and automated attacks. And now AI tools make it easier to produce convincing fake documents and faces. So the defenders need better data and better models too.

speaker: NORA
text: And we haven't mentioned the other well-known names.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right, there are other significant players in bureau and business data, for example CRIF and Dun and Bradstreet, but we didn't research them for this episode, so I won't make any claims about them.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's take stock. Where is Creditinfo with AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's an interesting mix of early and absent. Early, because back in July 2019 the company described an automated machine learning platform for bureaus, a system to generate predictive models more quickly. That was ahead of many companies at the time. But we don't see it on current product pages, so its status today is unknown. Our guess is that it may be dormant or folded into other products.

speaker: NORA
text: What would an automated machine learning platform for a bureau actually do?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, it speeds up building scorecards. A bureau or a lender wants a model that predicts the chance a borrower will default. Traditionally, a statistician builds that by hand over weeks: selecting variables, testing them, checking stability. An automated platform tries many combinations quickly and proposes the best-performing models, which experts then review. For a group running bureaus in many small markets, each needing its own models, that kind of tool could be very valuable.

speaker: NORA
text: So why might it have gone quiet?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't know. It could have become an internal tool rather than a product. It could have been overtaken by newer methods. Or it may simply not be marketed any more. But if it still exists inside the company, it's a foundation worth dusting off. That's our speculation.

speaker: NORA
text: And now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Now, the AI-labelled items we found are mostly through partners. The Lucinity partnership is framed around AI workflows, but that's Lucinity's AI using Creditinfo's data. There's a thought leadership piece on the website about large language models in financial services, but we couldn't date it or read it. We didn't find a named AI product on the website, AI hires, an AI team or an AI budget.

speaker: NORA
text: So it has the data, but not the product.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the cleanest way to say it. Creditinfo's data asset is real: bureau data across many countries, with licences that are hard to copy. But from the outside, it hasn't turned that asset into AI features it owns and sells.

speaker: NORA
text: What about governance?

speaker: JAMES
text: This is a highly regulated business, so governance matters a lot. Credit data is personal financial data. Every bureau operates under data protection rules and financial regulation. In February and March 2026 the Icelandic Data Protection Authority published decisions involving Creditinfo's credit reporting. We only saw the titles, not the content, so I don't know what they concluded. But it's a reminder that regulators watch this industry closely.

speaker: NORA
text: And AI-specific rules?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, the European Union's AI Act treats AI systems used to assess people's creditworthiness as high risk, which brings extra requirements around data quality, documentation, transparency and human oversight. Creditinfo operates in several EU countries, including Latvia and Estonia. So any AI scoring product in Europe would need to be built with those rules in mind from day one. We didn't find any AI-specific governance publicly, nor did we search for security certifications, so I can't say what's in place.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a fairness angle, like we discussed with Resolution Economics?

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much. Credit scoring decides who gets access to money. If a model is biased against a particular group, it can deepen exclusion rather than reduce it. For a company whose mission is financial inclusion, getting fairness right isn't just compliance. It's the point of the business.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's list the challenges. What keeps leadership up at night, in your view?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, the product gap. As we said, a valuable data asset without owned AI products. Buyers of data businesses increasingly pay for the products and platforms built on the data, not just the data itself.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, partner dependence. Fraud capability comes through Equifax Kount and NOTO. AI compliance workflows come through Lucinity. That's a fast way to get capability, but it means sharing margin and not owning the intellectual property. That's our inference, since we don't know the commercial terms.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, integration. Uganda, Namibia, Estonia, Latvia, the CEMAC regional bureau, eleven Caribbean countries through EveryData. Each has its own systems, its own regulations, its own data formats and often its own language. Building one technology platform that serves all of them is a huge job, and it's a precondition for rolling out AI products across the group.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a people side to that integration?

speaker: JAMES
text: A big one. Each acquired bureau has its own team, its own culture and its own relationships with local regulators and lenders. Those relationships are valuable and fragile. Moving everyone onto a common platform, common processes and common products, without losing local trust or key people, is a delicate balance. The companies that do it well usually keep strong local leadership for relationships, while centralising the technology and product work.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, regulation. Data protection authorities, central banks, financial regulators and, in Europe, the AI Act. Every country has its own rules, and they're tightening. A company operating in dozens of markets has to manage a very complex compliance map.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, timing. At nearly six years into the hold, the AI story needs to be proven, not promised, before a sale process. That puts pressure on the next twelve to eighteen months.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a talent challenge as well?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd expect so. Building credit models and AI products requires data scientists and machine learning engineers who understand both the technology and the regulation. Those people are in demand everywhere. A group spread across many smaller markets may find it harder to attract them than a global giant would. That's our inference.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's flip to opportunities. If you were on the board, where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: The first is AI-assisted KYC, PEP and fraud alert triage, built on Creditinfo's own local data and sold to bank and microfinance clients as an API, which is a way for software systems to connect directly.

speaker: NORA
text: Explain alert triage.

speaker: JAMES
text: When a bank screens customers and transactions against watchlists and fraud rules, it gets alerts. Huge numbers of them, and most are false positives. A customer whose name is similar to a politically exposed person, a payment that looks unusual but is innocent. Compliance analysts have to review each one. That's slow and expensive. AI can help rank the alerts, explain why each was raised, pull the relevant data together and suggest whether it's likely to be real. The analyst still decides, but much faster.

speaker: NORA
text: And why should Creditinfo do it rather than Lucinity?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because Creditinfo has the local data, the business registries, the PEP lists and the credit files in its markets. Clients already consume that data in AI workflows, as the Lucinity partnership shows. If Creditinfo owns the triage layer, at least for its own markets, it captures margin that currently flows to partners. That's our inference about the economics.

speaker: NORA
text: Wouldn't that annoy Lucinity, a partner?

speaker: JAMES
text: Possibly, and it's a real tension. One way through, in my view, is to focus on the markets and customer types where Creditinfo is strongest, for example smaller banks and microfinance institutions in its bureau countries, which may never buy a full compliance platform. Another is to make the triage capability available inside partners' platforms too, as a premium data product. Either way, the aim is to sell an answer, not just raw data.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, own more of the fraud layer. Pair the Equifax Kount platform with local bureau data and an in-house scoring layer, so Creditinfo adds its own value rather than just reselling.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, cross-selling across the new footprint. Take EveryData's consumer bureau and advisory products and combine them with Creditinfo's business information and decisioning products across the Caribbean. And fourth, geographic expansion. The company has said it's exploring Africa and the Middle East for the Equifax partnership, and it already has a presence in the Gulf.

speaker: NORA
text: And more acquisitions?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, more bureau roll-ups where the global players are stepping back from smaller markets. The pattern from 2023 to 2026 suggests that's a deliberate strategy. Sixth, alternative data scoring for thin-file borrowers, through mobile money and fintech partners like the Kenyan ones. And seventh, pricing. Moving from charging per report to usage-based pricing through APIs, which fits how digital lenders actually work. We didn't find any pricing data, so that's our suggestion.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the decisioning software? Is there an AI angle there?

speaker: JAMES
text: A big one, in my view. Imagine a lender's credit manager asking the decisioning system, in plain language: "Why did approvals in the northern region fall last month?" Or, "What happens to our default rate if we raise the approval threshold for first-time borrowers?" A generative AI analyst built into the decisioning software, working on the lender's own data and the bureau data, could answer those questions in minutes. For small lenders without big analytics teams, that's very valuable.

speaker: NORA
text: One AI bet for the next eighteen months. What is it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: AI-assisted KYC, PEP and fraud alert triage on Creditinfo's local data, delivered as an API. The value is analyst hours saved per alert for clients, plus revenue from a new product. It builds directly on data clients already use, and it moves Creditinfo up from data feed to workflow.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Let's walk through it. An invented bank.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Picture a mid-sized bank in Latvia, call it Daugava Bank. Its compliance team of eight analysts reviews hundreds of screening alerts a day. Most are false positives: a customer called Jānis Bērziņš whose name partly matches a politically exposed person's relative, a company whose director shares a name with someone on a sanctions list.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And today each alert means what?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Today an analyst opens the alert, looks up the customer, searches the business registry, checks the watchlist entry, compares dates of birth and addresses, and writes a short note explaining why it's a false positive or why it needs escalation. Maybe ten or fifteen minutes each. Multiply by hundreds a day.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And with the triage tool?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: The alert arrives already enriched. The tool has pulled Creditinfo's data on the customer and the watchlist entry, compared the identifying details, and written a short draft explanation: "Name match only. Date of birth differs by twenty-two years. Customer's registered address and business history are unrelated to the listed person. Suggested: low risk, close." The analyst reads it, checks the evidence, and closes it in a minute. The tool ranks the genuinely suspicious alerts at the top of the queue, so the team spends its time where it matters.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And the regulator?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: The regulator needs to see that a human made the decision, that the reasoning is recorded, and that the system is tested and monitored. So every suggestion has to be explainable and logged, and the bank needs to be able to show how often the tool's suggestions were right. That's not a burden to bolt on later. It's part of the product.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Now the hundred days.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: First thirty days: choose the market and the partners. Pick one or two markets where Creditinfo has rich local data and the regulation is well understood, perhaps Latvia, where it now owns the bureau outright. Recruit three to five design partner banks or microfinance institutions with real alert volumes. Agree the success measures: time per alert, false positives correctly closed, genuine risks caught. Settle the data rules, including how the tool complies with data protection law and, for credit-related uses, the AI Act.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Then?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days thirty to sixty: build and test on history. Take a sample of past alerts from the design partners, where the final decisions are known. Run the tool on them. Where does it agree with the analysts? Where does it disagree, and who was right? Tune it, and set the threshold for what it can suggest closing.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And the last stretch?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days sixty to a hundred: shadow mode. On live alerts, the tool makes suggestions alongside the analysts' normal work, without changing the process. Measure the time it would save and the accuracy. At day one hundred, decide on a launch, a price per alert or a subscription, and the next markets.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And who owns it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: A product leader with a clear mandate across data, technology and commercial, reporting close to the chief executive. With his background running a large bureau business, the chief executive is well placed to sponsor it. But someone has to own it day to day.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And this needs the integration work you mentioned.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: It does, but it doesn't have to wait for all of it. Starting in one or two markets lets the team prove the product while the wider platform work continues. Then each newly integrated market becomes a new place to sell it.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned a generative AI analyst inside the decisioning software. Let's walk through that too, because I think it shows a different side of the opportunity. Another invented example.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Picture a microfinance institution in Uganda, call it Kyaka Finance. It lends to small farmers and traders. It has a credit manager, call her Ruth, and a tiny analytics team of one person, who is also responsible for the monthly reports to the board and the regulator.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And what's Ruth's problem?
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Arrears are rising in one region, and she doesn't know why. Today, she asks her one analyst to pull the numbers. He exports data from the decisioning system and the loan book into spreadsheets, spends two days cutting it by product, branch, loan size and borrower type, and comes back with a few charts. By then the board meeting is close, and there's no time to test any ideas.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And with the AI analyst?
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Ruth types a question into the decisioning software. "Why are arrears rising in the western region this quarter?" The assistant looks at Kyaka's own loan data and the bureau data, within the rules on what it's allowed to see. It comes back with a short answer and charts. Most of the increase is in loans to first-time borrowers made in two branches. Those borrowers were approved at a higher average amount than in other branches. And bureau data shows that a larger share of them had other active loans with digital lenders at the time.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: So it's spotted that people were borrowing from several places at once.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly, which is a classic risk in fast-growing digital lending markets. Ruth then asks a follow-up. "What would have happened to approvals and arrears if we'd capped first-time loans at the regional average?" The assistant runs a simple scenario on historic data and shows the trade-off: fewer loans approved, lower arrears. Ruth takes that to the board, with her own judgment on top.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And where's the human in that?
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Everywhere that matters. Ruth decides what to ask and what to do. The assistant does the slicing and the first draft of the analysis. Her one analyst stops spending days on spreadsheets and spends his time checking the findings and thinking about policy. For a small institution, that's like adding an analytics team it could never afford to hire.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What does it need to work?
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Three things, in my view. Clean, consistent data, which brings us back to the integration challenge. Clear rules on what the assistant can access, especially bureau data about people who aren't Kyaka's customers. And explanations that a credit manager can check, so she isn't asked to trust a black box. If those are in place, it's a product many small lenders would pay for, and it's one that only a company with both bureau data and decisioning software can offer.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: So it plays to Creditinfo's unusual combination.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the point. A pure AI company doesn't have the bureau data. A pure bureau doesn't have the decisioning workflow. Creditinfo has both, at least in some markets. That's a real right to win, if it builds the product.
chapter: The lender's analyst, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other businesses learn from Creditinfo?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd pull out four lessons. First, where the giants retreat, specialists can win. Creditinfo has built a business in markets that the global players found too small or too complex. Many industries have equivalent corners.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, data is not the same as a product. Owning valuable data is a great start, but in the AI era, value increasingly flows to whoever owns the workflow where decisions are made. If you're a data company, ask where your data is used, and whether you could own that step.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, partnerships are a fast start, not a finish. Partnering with Equifax, Lucinity and NOTO brought capabilities quickly. But at some point, a company has to decide which of those capabilities it wants to own, because that's where the margin and the long-term value sit.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, build governance into the product from the start, especially in regulated markets. Explainability, logging, human oversight and fairness testing are much easier to design in than to retrofit, and in credit and compliance, they're what customers and regulators will ask for first.

speaker: NORA
text: I'll add one from the outside. Purpose can be a strategy.

speaker: JAMES
text: I agree. Creditinfo's mission is financial inclusion. That's not just a nice line. It's why governments choose it to run regional bureaus, and it points straight at the right AI products: better scoring for people who have been invisible to lenders.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI-native KYC and decisioning platforms taking the customer relationship and reducing the bureau to a commodity data feed. That's our inference. Two, global bureaus with bigger AI budgets competing in the same markets. Three, data protection rulings and the EU AI Act's high-risk rules restricting how credit models can be built and used. Four, open banking and alternative data reducing lenders' reliance on traditional bureau files.

speaker: NORA
text: Explain open banking quickly.

speaker: JAMES
text: Open banking lets customers share their bank account data directly with other providers, with consent, through secure connections. A lender could look at your actual income and spending instead of only your credit history. That's a competitor to bureau data in some uses, and also an opportunity, if a bureau can combine the two.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owner?

speaker: JAMES
text: Five, exit timing. Nearly six years into the hold, a buyer will want proof that the data can become AI-era products and revenue. And six, integration risk across a growing number of countries, each with its own systems and regulators.

speaker: NORA
text: Are there risks that come simply from operating in frontier markets?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, as general background. Currency swings can change what revenue earned in local currency is worth in euros or dollars. Political change can alter how regulators treat credit bureaus, or who wins the next tender for a national bureau. And economic shocks can raise default rates sharply, which hurts lenders and can squeeze their spending on data and software. A group spread across many such markets diversifies those risks, but it can't eliminate them. We didn't find any specific issues of this kind for Creditinfo. It's simply part of the territory.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch for?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four things. First, a named AI product launch from Creditinfo itself, rather than through a partner. Second, how EveryData is integrated across the Caribbean. Third, whether the Equifax partnership expands to Africa and the Middle East. And fourth, any more bureau acquisitions from the global players.

speaker: NORA
text: And a bonus?

speaker: JAMES
text: Any AI or technology leadership hire. That would be a strong signal that the company is moving from partner-led to owned AI.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: What does Creditinfo really sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: The ability to decide who to trust with money, in markets where that's hard.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Licensed credit bureaus and data in markets the giants have left.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: No named AI product of its own, as far as public evidence shows.

speaker: NORA
text: Best partnership?

speaker: JAMES
text: Lucinity, because it proves clients want its data inside AI workflows.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: AI alert triage for KYC, PEP and fraud, on its own data, sold as an API.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI replace credit bureaus?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. AI needs data, and bureaus have it. But AI could change who captures the value.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a lender in a frontier market should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Look at how many applicants you decline for thin files, and test whether alternative data would change those decisions.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Optimist. The data and the licences are real. It needs to own more of the product built on them.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. Creditinfo was founded in Iceland in 1997 by Reynir Grétarsson and now describes itself as London-based. It runs credit bureaus and sells credit data, fraud and identity checks and decisioning software, mainly in emerging and frontier markets, with bureau operations in around twenty-three countries and about four hundred and eighty staff, by its own count. Levine Leichtman bought a majority stake in March 2021, and since then it has bought bureaus from Experian in Uganda, Namibia and Estonia, taken full control of KIB Latvia, begun running the CEMAC regional bureau and acquired EveryData in the Caribbean. Its chief executive, Satrajit Saha, previously ran TransUnion Europe. Its fraud and AI compliance capabilities mostly come through partners like Equifax, Lucinity and NOTO. Its data asset is strong, but it lacks a named AI product. The best first move is AI-assisted KYC and fraud alert triage on its own data, built with governance from the start, before a future sale asks for proof.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the wider lesson is that in the AI era, owning the data gets you into the room. Owning the decision is what keeps you there.
